prompt:
Some people believe that university education should be free for all students and paid for by the government.

To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
outline: Quan điểm: không đồng ý phần lớn (không nên miễn phí cho tất cả). Mở bài: nêu bối cảnh học phí tăng, đưa quan điểm rõ ràng. Thân bài 1: thừa nhận lợi ích của miễn phí (mở rộng cơ hội cho sinh viên nghèo, lợi ích cho nền kinh tế). Thân bài 2: nhược điểm (người không học đại học vẫn phải đóng thuế, ngân sách hạn chế dẫn tới giảm chất lượng). Thân bài 3: giải pháp cân bằng (học bổng cho sinh viên khó khăn, khoản vay trả theo thu nhập). Kết bài: nhắc lại quan điểm.

for: Giúp sinh viên nghèo có cơ hội học đại học dựa trên năng lực
Lực lượng lao động có trình độ cao thúc đẩy kinh tế và đổi mới
Sinh viên không phải gánh nợ lớn sau khi tốt nghiệp
against: Người thu nhập thấp không học đại học vẫn phải trả thuế cho người khác học
Ngân sách hạn chế dẫn tới giới hạn chỉ tiêu hoặc chất lượng giảm
Hỗ trợ có mục tiêu (học bổng, vay theo thu nhập) công bằng và hiệu quả hơn

model:
In many countries, the cost of a degree has risen so sharply that students graduate with debts that take decades to repay. This has led some to argue that the state should cover tuition fees for everyone. While I accept that higher education brings wide social benefits, I believe that making it completely free for all students is neither fair nor sustainable.

The strongest argument for free tuition is that it widens access. Talented young people from low-income families are often put off by the prospect of heavy loans, and a free system would allow them to compete on merit rather than wealth. Moreover, a highly educated workforce benefits the whole economy, since graduates tend to earn more, pay more tax and drive innovation. From this perspective, public funding is an investment rather than a cost.

However, a fully free system has serious drawbacks. Universities are expensive to run, and if the government pays every fee, the money must come from general taxation, including taxes paid by people who never attend university and often earn less than graduates. This effectively asks lower earners to subsidise the future careers of the middle class. In addition, when funding is limited, free systems frequently respond by capping student numbers or allowing teaching quality to decline, as overcrowded lecture halls in some European countries show.

A more balanced approach would be to combine generous grants for students from poorer backgrounds with income-linked loans for others, which are repaid only once graduates earn above a certain threshold. This protects access without placing the entire burden on taxpayers.

In conclusion, although the aim of free higher education is admirable, I disagree that it should be provided to all students. Targeted support is a fairer and more effective way to ensure that ability, not income, determines who goes to university.

To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
outline: Quan điểm: không đồng ý. Mở bài: nêu xu hướng chính trị gia hứa hình phạt nặng hơn, đưa quan điểm. Thân bài 1: nhượng bộ (án dài bảo vệ xã hội khỏi tội phạm nguy hiểm, thể hiện sự nghiêm khắc). Thân bài 2: phản bác (án dài ít có tác dụng răn đe vì tội phạm thường bốc đồng, khả năng bị bắt quan trọng hơn mức án; nhà tù làm tăng tái phạm). Thân bài 3: giải pháp thay thế (tăng cảnh sát, đào tạo nghề trong tù, xử lý nguyên nhân gốc, ví dụ Na Uy). Kết bài.

for: Tội phạm nguy hiểm bị cách ly, xã hội an toàn hơn

Có thể răn đe một số người tính toán trước khi phạm tội
against: Phần lớn tội phạm hành động bốc đồng, không tính đến mức án
Khả năng bị bắt có tác dụng răn đe mạnh hơn mức độ hình phạt
Nhà tù khiến người phạm tội có thêm quan hệ tội phạm, tỉ lệ tái phạm cao
Phòng ngừa và cải tạo hiệu quả lâu dài hơn

model:
Many politicians respond to public concern about crime by promising tougher punishment, and longer prison terms are often presented as the obvious solution. Although I agree that serious offenders must be removed from society, I disagree that lengthening sentences is the most effective way to cut crime overall.

Admittedly, long sentences have some value. While dangerous criminals are behind bars, they cannot harm the public, and for violent or repeat offenders this protection is essential. Severe penalties also send a clear message that society takes certain crimes seriously, which may reassure victims and their families.

However, the evidence that longer sentences deter crime is weak. Most offenders do not calculate the length of a possible sentence before acting; they commit crimes impulsively, under the influence of drugs or alcohol, or because they believe they will not be caught. Research in criminology consistently suggests that the certainty of being caught matters far more than the severity of the punishment. Furthermore, prisons can make the problem worse. Inmates who spend years mixing with hardened criminals often leave with fewer job prospects and stronger criminal connections, so reoffending rates remain high.

For these reasons, resources would be better spent elsewhere. More visible policing increases the chance of arrest, while education and job-training programmes inside prisons help former inmates find legal work after release. Tackling root causes such as poverty, school dropout and addiction would also prevent many young people from turning to crime in the first place. Norway, for example, combines relatively short sentences with intensive rehabilitation and has one of the lowest reoffending rates in Europe.

In conclusion, while prison remains necessary for the most dangerous offenders, simply making sentences longer is not the best way to reduce crime. Prevention, effective policing and rehabilitation offer far greater long-term benefits.

prompt:
Governments should spend money on improving public transport rather than on building new roads.

To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
outline: Quan điểm: đồng ý mạnh (ở khu vực đô thị). Mở bài: bối cảnh ngân sách giao thông hạn chế, nêu quan điểm. Thân bài 1: đường mới không giải quyết ùn tắc lâu dài (nhu cầu phát sinh), giao thông công cộng chở nhiều người hơn trên ít diện tích hơn, ví dụ metro TP.HCM. Thân bài 2: lợi ích môi trường và xã hội (ít khí thải, người không có xe vẫn đi lại được). Thân bài 3: nhượng bộ (nông thôn và vận tải hàng hóa vẫn cần đường) nhưng đó là ngoại lệ. Kết bài.

for: Đường mới nhanh chóng bị lấp đầy (induced demand)
Metro, xe buýt nhanh chở nhiều người hơn, tốn ít diện tích
Giảm khí thải và ô nhiễm không khí
Giúp người già, sinh viên, người thu nhập thấp đi lại
against: Nông thôn dân cư thưa không có lựa chọn thay thế ô tô
Hàng hóa vẫn cần vận chuyển bằng xe tải
Đường hiện có cần được bảo trì, một số tuyến mới vẫn cần thiết

model:
As cities grow, governments face a difficult choice about how to spend limited transport budgets. Some argue that new roads are needed to keep traffic moving, but I strongly agree that investment in public transport should be the priority, at least in urban areas.

The main reason is that building more roads rarely solves congestion for long. Wider roads make driving more attractive, so more people choose to travel by car and the new capacity quickly fills up, a pattern known as induced demand. In contrast, a single metro line or bus rapid transit route can carry tens of thousands of passengers an hour while occupying far less space than the equivalent number of cars. Ho Chi Minh City's first metro line, for instance, offers commuters an alternative to roads that are already saturated with motorbikes.

Public transport also brings environmental and social benefits. Fewer private vehicles mean lower emissions and cleaner air, which matters in cities where pollution is a growing health concern. Furthermore, affordable buses and trains give mobility to people who cannot drive or cannot afford a car, such as students, the elderly and low-income workers, allowing them to reach jobs and services.

Of course, roads cannot be ignored entirely. Rural areas with scattered populations may have no realistic alternative to cars, and goods still need to be transported by lorry. Existing roads must therefore be maintained, and in some regions new links may be justified. However, these are exceptions rather than a reason to make road building the main focus of spending.

In conclusion, I believe governments should direct most of their transport investment towards public transport. It moves more people more efficiently, reduces pollution and makes cities fairer, whereas new roads tend to offer only a temporary solution.

prompt:

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

outline: Quan điểm: AI sẽ tạo thêm việc làm về lâu dài, nhưng cần hỗ trợ người lao động. Mở bài: AI làm được nhiều việc của con người, nêu hai quan điểm và ý kiến cá nhân. Thân bài 1: quan điểm lo ngại thất nghiệp (AI thay cả lao động văn phòng, thay đổi quá nhanh để kịp đào tạo lại). Thân bài 2: quan điểm tạo việc làm (lịch sử máy tính, nghề mới về dữ liệu và AI, giải phóng con người khỏi việc lặp lại). Thân bài 3: ý kiến cá nhân và đề xuất (đào tạo lại, đổi chương trình học). Kết bài.

for: Công nghệ trước đây thay đổi chứ không xóa bỏ việc làm (ví dụ máy tính văn phòng)
Xuất hiện nghề mới: chuyên gia dữ liệu, người huấn luyện và kiểm thử AI

against: AI thay thế cả công việc văn phòng: tổng đài, dịch thuật, kế toán
Tốc độ thay đổi quá nhanh, người lao động không kịp đào tạo lại
Doanh nghiệp dùng AI chủ yếu để cắt giảm chi phí nhân sự

model:
Artificial intelligence is now able to write reports, analyse data and answer customer queries, tasks that until recently required human workers. Opinion is divided over whether this will destroy jobs or create new ones. In my view, AI will create new kinds of work, but only if societies help workers adapt.

Those who fear unemployment point out that AI can replace not only manual labour but also white-collar roles. Call centre staff, translators and junior accountants already face competition from software that works faster and more cheaply. Unlike earlier machines, AI systems can be updated and copied instantly, so change may happen too quickly for workers to retrain. If companies use automation mainly to cut costs, many people in their forties and fifties could find their skills suddenly worth very little.

On the other hand, history suggests that technology tends to transform jobs rather than eliminate work altogether. When computers became common in offices, typists disappeared, but millions of new roles appeared in software, digital marketing and IT support. Similarly, AI is already generating demand for data specialists, people who train and test AI systems, and professionals who combine expertise in a field such as medicine or law with the ability to use these tools. AI can also take over repetitive tasks, freeing employees to focus on creative and interpersonal work that machines handle poorly.

I believe the second view is more convincing in the long term, yet the transition could be painful. Governments and employers should therefore invest in affordable retraining and update school curricula so that young people learn to work alongside AI rather than compete with it.

In conclusion, while AI will undoubtedly make some jobs obsolete, it is likely to create more opportunities overall, provided that workers are given the support they need to adjust.

model:
Since the pandemic, millions of employees have discovered that they can do their jobs from home, and many are reluctant to return to the office full-time. While some argue that remote work benefits everyone, others insist that offices remain essential. I believe that a combination of the two is the most effective arrangement.

Supporters of working from home emphasise flexibility and time savings. Without a daily commute, which can take two hours in a congested city, employees have more energy for work and family life. Many report that they concentrate better at home, away from the constant interruptions of an open-plan office. Employers can also benefit, as they spend less on office space and can recruit talented people who live far from headquarters, or even in another country.

However, there are strong arguments for the office. Much learning happens informally, when junior staff watch experienced colleagues handle a difficult client or ask a quick question across the desk. This is far harder over video calls, so young employees working remotely may develop more slowly. Offices also encourage spontaneous conversations that lead to new ideas, and they create a sense of belonging that keeps staff loyal to the company. Furthermore, not everyone has a quiet room at home, and for some people the boundary between work and private life disappears, leading to longer hours and burnout.

In my opinion, the best solution is a hybrid model. Employees could spend two or three days a week in the office for meetings, training and teamwork, and work from home on days that require deep concentration. This keeps most of the benefits of both systems.

In conclusion, both remote and office work have clear advantages, but neither is ideal on its own. A flexible hybrid arrangement allows organisations to balance productivity, wellbeing and collaboration.

model:
Space programmes cost billions of dollars every year, and at a time when many countries struggle with poverty, climate change and ageing populations, their value is often questioned. Some people believe this money should be redirected to problems on Earth, while others defend space research. In my view, space exploration deserves continued funding, although at a modest and carefully justified level.

Critics argue that it is difficult to justify sending probes to Mars when millions of people lack clean water, healthcare or decent housing. Public money is limited, and every dollar spent on rockets is a dollar not spent on hospitals or schools. From this perspective, governments have a moral duty to address urgent human suffering before pursuing scientific curiosity, especially since the benefits of space missions can seem distant and abstract to ordinary taxpayers.

On the other hand, space research often helps to solve the very problems that critics mention. Satellites allow scientists to monitor deforestation, track storms and measure rising sea levels, providing data that is essential for tackling climate change. Technologies first developed for space programmes, such as water purification systems and improved medical imaging, have later been used in everyday life. In addition, space missions inspire young people to study science and engineering, which strengthens a nation's economy in the long run.

I believe the second argument is stronger, because the choice is not really between space and Earth. Space budgets usually represent a very small share of public spending, and cutting them would make little difference to healthcare or education. However, governments should ensure that missions have clear scientific or practical goals rather than serving mainly as symbols of national prestige.

In conclusion, although problems on Earth must remain the priority, a reasonable investment in space exploration is justified by its practical, scientific and educational benefits.

outline: Quan điểm: lợi ích lớn hơn. Mở bài: xu hướng mua thực phẩm địa phương, nêu quan điểm. Thân bài 1: lợi ích môi trường và sức khỏe (giảm quãng đường vận chuyển, ít bao bì, tươi hơn). model:
Campaigns encouraging consumers to buy locally grown food have become popular in many countries, often promoted as a way to protect the environment and support farmers. Although this trend has some drawbacks, I believe its advantages are greater.

The most obvious benefit is environmental. Food imported from other continents is often transported by air or refrigerated ship, which produces significant carbon emissions. Buying from nearby farms reduces these 'food miles' and usually requires less packaging, since the produce does not need protection during long journeys. Local food also tends to be fresher, because it is harvested closer to the time it is sold, so it often retains more flavour and nutrients.

There are economic and social benefits as well. When consumers spend money at farmers' markets or on regional products, more of that money stays in the local community, helping small farms survive against competition from large agricultural companies. This preserves rural jobs and traditional farming knowledge, and it allows people to know where their food comes from and how it was produced.

Nevertheless, the disadvantages should not be ignored. Local food can be more expensive, particularly for low-income families, and choice becomes limited in winter or in countries with harsh climates. Moreover, the environmental argument is not always straightforward: tomatoes grown in heated greenhouses in northern Europe may generate more emissions than those shipped from sunny Spain. Finally, if every country bought only its own produce, farmers in developing nations who depend on exports would lose vital income.

On balance, however, these problems can be managed. Consumers do not need to avoid imports completely; choosing local, seasonal food where possible brings most of the benefits without the costs.

In conclusion, while buying local food is not a perfect solution, its environmental, economic and health benefits outweigh its disadvantages, especially when combined with sensible seasonal choices.

model:
Thanks to digital platforms, more and more people now earn a living as freelancers or on short-term contracts, from graphic designers and translators to delivery riders. While this shift offers greater freedom, I believe that for most workers its disadvantages outweigh its advantages.

There are certainly attractive aspects to this way of working. Freelancers can usually choose their own hours and projects, which suits parents with young children, students and people who want to travel. Highly skilled professionals, such as software developers, can often earn more by working for several clients than they would in a single salaried position. For businesses, contract workers provide flexibility, allowing them to hire specialists for particular projects without the long-term cost of a permanent employee.

However, these benefits are not shared equally. For many people, especially those in low-paid platform work, freelancing means an unpredictable income that makes it difficult to plan, rent a flat or obtain a bank loan. Unlike permanent employees, freelancers rarely receive paid holidays, sick pay or pension contributions, so a period of illness or a few quiet months can quickly lead to financial difficulty. There are also hidden costs. Workers must find their own clients, manage their own taxes and update their skills at their own expense, and many report feeling isolated without colleagues.

These problems suggest that the trend benefits employers and a minority of highly skilled workers far more than the majority. Unless governments update labour laws to give freelancers basic protections, such as minimum rates and access to social insurance, the flexibility they enjoy comes at too high a price.

In conclusion, although freelance and contract work offer genuine freedom and flexibility, the loss of security and benefits that comes with them means that, for most people, the disadvantages are greater.

model:
Wearable devices and health apps have moved from being gadgets for athletes to everyday tools for millions of ordinary people. Although these technologies raise some concerns, I believe their advantages clearly outweigh their disadvantages.

The main benefit is that they encourage healthier habits. When people can see exactly how many steps they have taken or how little they have slept, they become more aware of their lifestyle, and simple features such as reminders to stand up or daily activity goals can motivate them to change. In addition, these devices can sometimes detect serious problems early. There have been many reported cases of smartwatches warning users about an irregular heartbeat, prompting them to see a doctor before a condition became dangerous. For patients with chronic illnesses such as diabetes, continuous monitoring also allows doctors to adjust treatment based on real data rather than occasional clinic visits.

There are, however, some drawbacks. The data produced by consumer devices is not always accurate, and some users may become anxious about minor fluctuations or try to diagnose themselves instead of seeking professional advice. Privacy is another concern, as health information is extremely sensitive, and companies could share or sell it to advertisers or insurers. Finally, the best devices are expensive, so the people who might benefit most, such as older or low-income patients, are often the least likely to own them.

Nevertheless, these problems can largely be addressed. Stronger data protection laws can limit how companies use personal information, and doctors can help patients interpret their data sensibly. As prices fall, the technology is also becoming more accessible.

In conclusion, despite concerns about accuracy, privacy and cost, health-monitoring technology brings significant benefits in prevention and early diagnosis, so I believe its advantages outweigh its disadvantages.

Thân bài 2: giải pháp (cấm/đánh thuế đồ nhựa dùng một lần, cải thiện thu gom rác ở thành phố ven biển, hoàn tiền vỏ chai, trách nhiệm nhà sản xuất). Kết bài: tóm tắt.

model:
Millions of tonnes of plastic enter the oceans every year, carried by rivers, washed off beaches or dumped from ships. This pollution causes serious harm to marine life and human health, but a combination of government action, business responsibility and public effort could significantly reduce it.

The most visible problem is the damage to wildlife. Sea turtles, birds and whales often mistake plastic bags and fragments for food, and once their stomachs are filled with indigestible material, they starve. Others become trapped in abandoned fishing nets and drown. A less visible but equally worrying issue is microplastics. As larger items break down into tiny particles, they are absorbed by fish and shellfish and eventually enter the human food chain, with possible long-term effects on health that scientists are only beginning to understand. Plastic waste also damages economies that depend on tourism and fishing, as polluted beaches deter visitors and reduce catches.

Several measures could tackle this problem. First, governments should reduce the production of unnecessary plastic by banning or taxing single-use items such as bags, straws and food containers. Several countries that have introduced charges for plastic bags have seen their use fall dramatically. Second, waste collection must be improved, particularly in fast-growing coastal cities where much ocean plastic originates. Investment in recycling facilities and deposit-return schemes for bottles would prevent waste from reaching rivers in the first place. Finally, manufacturers could be made legally responsible for collecting and recycling the packaging they produce, which would encourage them to design products that use less plastic. Individuals can support these efforts by carrying reusable bags and bottles.

In conclusion, plastic pollution threatens marine ecosystems, human health and coastal economies. Reducing plastic use, improving waste management and holding producers accountable are the most effective ways to address the problem.

Thân bài 2: giải pháp (thuế đồ uống có đường, hạn chế quảng cáo; trường học có bữa ăn dinh dưỡng, một giờ vận động; cha mẹ được cung cấp thông tin, thêm công viên). Kết bài.

Thiếu không gian an toàn để chơi, áp lực học tập giảm thời gian thể thao

model:
Childhood obesity has risen sharply in recent decades, not only in wealthy nations but also in rapidly developing countries such as Vietnam and China. This trend has several causes linked to modern lifestyles, but families, schools and governments can all play a part in reversing it.

The main cause is a change in diet. Processed foods, sugary drinks and fast food are now cheaper and more widely available than ever, and they are heavily advertised to children through television and social media. Busy parents who work long hours often rely on these convenient options instead of preparing home-cooked meals. At the same time, children are far less active than previous generations. Many spend hours each day on phones, tablets and computer games, while in crowded cities there is little safe space for outdoor play. In some education systems, pressure to perform well academically has also reduced the time available for sport and physical education.

Tackling this problem requires action at several levels. Governments could introduce a tax on sugary drinks, as the United Kingdom and Mexico have done, and restrict advertisements for unhealthy food during children's programmes. Schools have an important role too. They should provide nutritious meals, remove vending machines selling snacks and fizzy drinks, and guarantee at least one hour of physical activity each day. Finally, parents need better information about nutrition, and local authorities could create more parks and sports facilities so that children have safe places to exercise.

In conclusion, rising childhood obesity is mainly the result of unhealthy diets and inactive lifestyles. A combination of government regulation, healthier school environments and greater parental awareness offers the best chance of helping children grow up at a healthy weight.

model:
In many of the world's largest cities, from Jakarta to London, roads are blocked by traffic for much of the day. This congestion creates economic, environmental and health problems, but a range of practical solutions could ease it.

The first problem is wasted time and money. Commuters who spend two or three hours a day in traffic have less time for work, rest and family, and businesses lose productivity when deliveries and employees arrive late. Congestion also worsens air pollution. Vehicles stuck in slow-moving traffic burn fuel inefficiently and release large amounts of exhaust fumes, contributing to respiratory diseases such as asthma, particularly among children and older people. In addition, long journeys in heavy traffic raise stress levels and can make drivers more aggressive, increasing the risk of accidents.

Several measures could reduce the problem. The most effective long-term solution is to provide fast, reliable and affordable public transport, such as metro systems and dedicated bus lanes, so that people have a genuine alternative to private vehicles. Second, governments could introduce congestion charges, requiring drivers to pay to enter the city centre at peak times. Singapore and Stockholm have used this approach successfully to reduce traffic and raise money for public transport. Third, urban planning can make a difference. Building homes, offices and shops closer together, and creating safe cycle lanes and pavements, would mean that more short journeys could be made on foot or by bicycle. Employers could also help by allowing flexible hours or remote work, which spreads traffic more evenly across the day.

In conclusion, traffic congestion harms economies, health and quality of life. Better public transport, road pricing and smarter urban planning together offer the best way to keep cities moving.

model:
Reports in many countries suggest that a growing proportion of crimes, from shoplifting to online fraud, are committed by teenagers and young adults. This trend has a number of social and economic causes, but it can be addressed through support from families, schools and communities.

One major reason is a lack of opportunity. In areas with high youth unemployment, young people who leave school without qualifications may see little chance of earning a decent income legally, and crime can appear to offer quick money and status. Family problems also play a role. Children who grow up with little supervision, perhaps because their parents work long hours or the family has broken down, are more easily influenced by older peers or gangs. Furthermore, the internet has created new temptations. Social media can glamorise violence and luxury lifestyles, and young people with digital skills may be drawn into cybercrime, which they often do not regard as seriously as physical theft.

Preventing youth crime requires early intervention rather than punishment alone. Schools should identify students who are falling behind or are frequently absent and provide them with mentoring, since dropping out of education is closely linked to offending. Communities can offer affordable sports clubs, music programmes and youth centres that give teenagers a positive way to spend their free time and build self-esteem. Governments could also fund apprenticeships and vocational training so that young people without academic qualifications have a realistic path into work. For those who have already offended, programmes that make them repair the harm they have caused, rather than sending them to adult prisons, are more likely to change their behaviour.

In conclusion, youth crime is driven mainly by limited opportunities, weak family support and new online influences. Early support, constructive activities and routes into employment are the most effective ways to prevent it.

In most cities today, it is common to see people looking at their phones while they walk, eat or wait for a bus. This habit has grown for several reasons, and although smartphones bring real benefits, I believe the amount of time people now spend on them is largely a negative development.

The main reason for this trend is that smartphones have become essential tools for everyday life. People use them to pay bills, order food, book taxis, communicate with colleagues and even attend online classes, so many tasks that once happened offline now require a screen. In addition, many apps are deliberately designed to be addictive. Social media platforms use endless scrolling, notifications and personalised recommendations to keep users engaged for as long as possible, because their profits depend on advertising.

Some of this screen time is clearly positive. Smartphones allow people to stay in touch with relatives abroad, access information instantly and learn new skills through educational apps and videos. For many workers, they also make flexible and remote work possible.

However, the negative effects are significant. Excessive use, particularly at night, disrupts sleep and has been linked to anxiety and depression, especially among teenagers who constantly compare themselves with others online. Constant notifications also reduce concentration, making it harder to read deeply or focus on demanding work. Perhaps most worryingly, phones can weaken face-to-face relationships, as families and friends sit together while each person is absorbed in their own screen.

In conclusion, people spend more time on smartphones because these devices have become central to daily life and because many apps are designed to capture attention. While the technology itself is useful, the current level of use is harmful overall, and individuals should make a conscious effort to limit unnecessary screen time.

In many countries, it is increasingly common for graduates to work in jobs that have little connection with their degree, or even to remain unemployed for long periods after leaving university. This situation has several causes, but universities can take practical steps to improve their students' prospects.

One reason is a mismatch between the number of graduates and the needs of the labour market. As higher education has expanded, more students are choosing popular subjects such as business administration, while there is a shortage of graduates in fields like engineering, nursing and data analysis. As a result, competition for jobs in crowded fields is intense. Another reason is that many degree programmes focus heavily on theory and fail to keep pace with changes in industry. Employers frequently complain that new graduates lack practical skills, such as using up-to-date software, communicating with clients or working in teams, and therefore prefer candidates with experience.

Universities can address these problems in several ways. First, they should work more closely with employers when designing courses, inviting companies to advise on content and to contribute guest lectures or real-world projects. Second, internships and work placements could become a compulsory part of every degree, so that students graduate with relevant experience and professional contacts. Third, universities should provide better careers guidance before students choose their major, including clear information about employment rates and typical salaries in different fields. This would help young people make more informed decisions rather than simply following trends or family pressure.

In conclusion, graduates struggle to find relevant work mainly because of an oversupply in certain subjects and a gap between academic study and workplace skills. Closer links with industry, compulsory work experience and better careers advice would make a university education far more useful for finding employment.
